title: Flow Matching for Offline Reinforcement Learning with Discrete Actions
claim: Continuous treatment of multimodal decisions interpolates between modes and collapses toward the mean, leading into a state never seen in the data.
layout: 2 panels, left-to-right, shared grid axes with colored arrows
description: Two side-by-side 2-D grid-world panels share the same layout. A black start dot sits at the bottom center. A red square trap state sits in the middle, and a green star (Goal A) and a crimson star (Goal B) mark the top corners. In the left panel, the offline data has two disjoint modes. Green arrows run left and then up to Goal A. Crimson arrows run right and then up to Goal B. Both routes avoid the trap. In the right panel, a single blue arrow path runs straight up from the start into the red trap. A blue X and a red 'mode collapse' label mark the failure. The red trap square and the colored arrows draw the eye first.
caption: Motivating example a) Offline dataset exhibits two disjoint modes corresponding to different objectives (Goal A and Goal B); the central region is a trap state never observed in the data. b) A continuous treatment of the decision space can induce interpolation between the modes and potential collapse toward the mean, causing trajectories to enter the trap.
abstract: Generative policies based on diffusion models and flow matching have shown strong promise for offline reinforcement learning (RL), but their applicability remains largely confined to continuous action spaces. To address a broader range of offline RL settings, we extend flow matching to a general framework that supports discrete action spaces with multiple objectives. Specifically, we replace continuous flows with continuous-time Markov chains, trained using a Q-weighted flow matching objective. We then extend our design to multi-agent settings, mitigating the exponential growth of joint action spaces via a factorized conditional path. For an oracle single policy-improvement step from the behavior distribution, we theoretically show that, under idealized conditions, the Q-weighted objective recovers the KL-regularized Boltzmann policy. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method performs robustly across diverse settings and benchmarks, including high-dimensional control, multi-agent games, and dynamically changing preferences over multiple objectives, while achieving competitive performance and demonstrating advantages in multimodal decision-making and preference-conditioned policy representation. Our discrete framework can also be applied to continuous-control problems through action quantization, providing a flexible trade-off between representational complexity and performance.
